title: Noise rules, trust ladder and shadow report

story: fcp already had a bot that opened pull requests: a weekly workflow that bumped dependencies. Every week a new PR appeared, and for a while people opened them. Then the PRs got bigger, some were red, and nobody had time. Of its last 14 pull requests, 13 were closed without a single review. The bot had taught the whole team one lesson: its PRs are safe to ignore.

Now the frontend CI fixer from the last lesson is ready to switch on. It is good, but not perfect. If it opens real pull requests on day one, and two of its first five are wrong, people will learn the same lesson about it, and its good PRs will be ignored too. Attention is the one thing a routine cannot buy back.
hook.question: How does a new routine earn people's attention step by step, and lose it fast when it misbehaves?

read.h: Three stages, from silent to trusted
p: Every routine sits on one step of a trust ladder, and its stage decides what it may do with a finished run. A new routine starts in shadow: it runs on real triggers, in a real VM, with the real harness, but it opens nothing. Its diff and its proof go to S3, our file storage on AWS, and nobody is pinged. In drafts, it opens real draft pull requests and pings only its owner, who may mark a good one ready. In normal, the routine marks its clean pull requests ready itself and asks the reviewer of the day. Even in normal, no agent approves or merges: a person always gives the one approval.

Shadow is the step that makes the whole ladder work, because it produces evidence at no cost to anyone's attention. Every Sunday a report puts each shadow fix next to what a person really did for the same failure, so the owner can see whether the routine would have helped. The stage itself lives in two places, which the next sections explain: the charter's stage: line, changed only by a reviewed pull request, and an override flag that can only lower it. A run uses the lower of the two.

notes.text: The order matters: the index is the height on the ladder.
Shadow still does all the work. Only the last step, showing it to people, is skipped.
The override can only make the stage lower, never higher. routineRun reads this at start and stores it in the Stage search attribute.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the weekly shadow report
p: Shadow helps only if someone looks at it. The report finds the human fix for each shadow run: for red main, the commits up to the next green build; for a bug, the merged PR linked to the ticket; for an update, what the Renovate PR became. If the human fix added tests, a small VM runs those tests on the routine's saved diff. That is the objective answer to "would it have worked?".

Then a Sonnet 5.5 judge at medium effort answers three short questions: the same root cause, a smaller or bigger change, and would a reviewer reject it. The judge is checked on 10 labelled pairs before anyone trusts it. One row per run goes to the weekly run review thread, never to the team channels.

read.h: Up slowly, on evidence, through a pull request
p: Moving up needs proof, and the proof is the same for every routine. Its slice of the routine bench, a set of past failures with known human fixes, must be at least 50% solved; a bug fixer must also reproduce at least 60% of its bugs. It must have zero false heals, which are fixes that turn CI green by weakening a test. And it must have at least 10 runs at its current stage, so one lucky week does not count.

A daily job checks every routine. When nothing is missing, it does not promote anything. It sends the owner a direct message: this routine qualifies for the next stage, open the charter PR if you agree. The owner opens a pull request that raises stage: in the charter, and someone else approves it, like any other change. Promotion is a person's decision with evidence attached, never a side effect of a script.

notes.text: The routine's bench slice, scored by the routine bench lesson.
Bug fixers must also show they found the same bug, not only a fix.
Ten runs is a starting value; it should be set from real data later.
An empty list means it qualifies. The daily job then tells the owner, nothing more.

read.h: Down at once, with a flag first
p: Moving down is the opposite: fast, automatic, one step. Three things count as misbehaviour. Any false heal. A revert within 14 days, meaning someone put a 'Revert "…"' commit on main that names one of the routine's merged PRs. Or fewer than half of its last 20 closed pull requests merged, which means people keep closing its work.

A pull request to the charter would take hours or days to be reviewed, and meanwhile the routine would keep running at the higher stage. So the daily job first writes an override flag, routine:<name>:stage_override, in the flag store that the kill switch also uses. The very next run reads the lower stage. Then the job opens a pull request that lowers stage: in the charter, so the file catches up and stays the truth, and it tells the owner why. The asymmetry is on purpose: one bad sign is enough to step down, but stepping up takes weeks of evidence and a person's yes.

notes.text: Only false heals since the last stage change, so an old one is not punished twice.
mergeRate is undefined with fewer than 20 closed PRs: no verdict on a handful.
Takes effect now: the next run reads the lower stage.
The file catches up through review.
Promotion only ever produces a message to the owner.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the noise rules under the ladder
p: Four small rules keep every routine quiet at every stage, and they ship before the first routine. A routine may have at most one open pull request; if one is open, the next run waits and checks again every hour on a Temporal timer. Every routine PR opens as a draft with the labels routine:<name> and agent. A routine PR with no commit, comment or review for 7 days is closed with a short note, and its Jira ticket gets a comment. Renovate's own PRs are not touched, because Renovate manages them itself.

Each team also gets one Slack digest a day instead of many pings: ready PRs waiting for review, drafts per owner, idle closes, paused routines with the reason, and yesterday's cost per routine. A quiet day sends nothing. And a routine whose merge rate drops under 50% of its last 20 closed PRs pauses itself and messages its owner, who resumes it with a button. The ladder reuses the same mergeRate function, so there is one definition of "people keep closing its work".

lab.title: One morning on the ladder
needs: Node 22.18 or newer (it runs .ts files directly)
lab.goal: Run the trust ladder's daily decision over five routines, write the promotion rule yourself, and see why the order of the two checks matters.

guess.q: be-ci-fixer is in normal. Its bench score is 62%, it has no false heals and 31 runs, but one of its merged PRs was reverted 9 days ago. What should the daily job do?

options.text: Nothing: the bench score and the run count are good, so it stays in normal.
options.why: A good score does not cancel a bad sign. A revert within 14 days is enough to step down.

options.text: Lower it to drafts now with the override flag, and open a PR that lowers stage: in the charter.
options.why: Demotion is one step, immediate through the flag, and then the file catches up through review.

options.text: Pause the routine until its owner looks.
options.why: Pausing is the circuit breaker's answer to repeated failed runs. One revert moves the routine one step down; it keeps running there.

lab.build: Write missingForPromotion in ladder.ts. It returns a list of reasons, and an empty list means the routine qualifies: the bench must be at least 50% solved; a routine of kind bug-fixer must also have reproduced at least 60%; there must be no false heals, on the bench or since the last stage change; and there must be at least 10 runs at the current stage. Use pct() for the percentages. Run node ladder-day.ts until every line is a decision. Then add a sixth routine to routines.json, a bug fixer in drafts with one false heal since its stage change, and check that it steps down to shadow.
checks: fe-ci-fixer: qualifies for drafts; DM the owner
fe-bug-fixer: stays shadow (reproduced 50% of bugs, needs 60%)
fe-upgrade-fixer: stays drafts (only 6 runs at this stage, needs 10)
The two demotions are unchanged: be-ci-fixer goes to drafts and fe-dead-code goes to shadow.
Your sixth routine prints drafts → shadow now (a false heal).
lab.fix: A teammate thought it was unfair that a routine with a great bench score could be demoted, so they moved the promotion check above the demotion check in decide. Add a routine in drafts with a 70% bench score, 15 runs, no false heals and one PR reverted 3 days ago, then swap the two checks the same way and run node ladder-day.ts. The job tells the owner that the routine qualifies for normal on the same morning that one of its fixes was reverted, and it is never stepped down. Put the checks back in the right order and explain why the way down must be checked first.
explain: Why does a new routine start in shadow, when it would be faster to let it open draft PRs from day one?
Why does a demotion write a flag first and open a charter PR second, while a promotion only sends a message?
missingForPromotion needs 10 runs at the current stage. What could go wrong if a routine could be promoted after its first good week?
lab.done: node ladder-day.ts prints one decision per routine, matching the checks, and you can say why demotion is checked before promotion.

check.q: A routine in shadow solves its bench well and has 15 clean runs. What happens to it?

options.text: The daily job moves it to drafts automatically
options.why: Promotion is never automatic. The job only tells the owner that the routine qualifies.

options.text: Its owner gets a message, opens a PR that raises stage: in the charter, and someone else approves it
options.why: Moving up is a person's decision, made in a reviewed pull request with the evidence attached.

options.text: It stays in shadow until the weekly report has a perfect week
options.why: The report gives the owner evidence, but the rule is the bench score, zero false heals and 10 runs, not a perfect week.

check.q: A routine in normal makes a fix that turns CI green by skipping a test, and the false-heal check catches it. What happens, and how fast?

options.text: It is paused until its owner presses Resume
options.why: Pausing is for a routine whose runs keep failing or whose PRs keep being closed. One false heal moves it one step down the ladder, and it keeps running there.

options.text: Nothing changes until the charter PR that lowers the stage is approved
options.why: Waiting for review would leave the routine at the higher stage for hours or days. The flag acts first.

options.text: The daily job writes the override flag, so the next run is at drafts, then opens a charter PR and tells the owner
options.why: Demotion is one step and immediate through the flag; the file catches up through review so it stays the truth.

check.q: Why does the trust ladder go up slowly but down fast?

options.text: Because one bad PR costs people's trust in all of the routine's PRs, while proving it is good takes many runs
options.why: Attention is easy to lose and hard to win back, so the ladder reacts to the first bad sign and asks for weeks of evidence before trusting more.

options.text: Because demotions are cheap to compute and promotions are expensive
options.why: Both are a few comparisons. The reason is about people's trust, not about compute.

options.text: Because routines usually get worse over time
options.why: Nothing suggests that. The asymmetry protects people's attention, whatever the routine's direction.

p: The noise rules come first, before any routine: orchestrator/src/activities/noise.ts with mayOpenPr (part of routineRun's pre-run gate; one open PR per routine, re-checked hourly) and closeIdlePrs (daily at 23 3 * * *, 7 idle days), all through the broker with an orchestrator scope that reads PRs and comments on and closes PRs labelled routine:*. digest.ts posts one Slack digest per team at 37 6 * * 0-4 Asia/Jerusalem to the channel in config/people.yaml, and holds mergeRate (last 20 closed PRs) and the auto-pause under 0.5 into routine:<name>:paused in the G3 flag store.

The ladder is orchestrator/src/routines/ladder.ts, called by a daily Temporal schedule for every routine. Bench scores come from the G1 eval results store. The effective stage is the lower of the charter's stage: and routine:<name>:stage_override; routineRun stores it in the Stage search attribute. The weekly shadow report, orchestrator/src/reports/shadow-report.ts, runs from the Sunday schedule and posts to the weekly run review thread.

tickets.why: One open PR per routine, drafts with the routine label, and the 7-day idle close.
The daily team digest, mergeRate, and the auto-pause under 50% merged.
The trust ladder: stages, the override flag, immediate demotion and owner-signed promotion.
The weekly shadow report: each shadow fix next to the human fix, with tests and a judge.

words.plain: The three stages a routine moves through, shadow, drafts and normal, which decide what it may do with a finished run.
The first stage: the routine runs on real triggers and saves its fix, but opens nothing and pings nobody.
A flag that lowers a routine's stage at once, before the charter PR that makes it permanent is reviewed.
A fix that turns CI green by weakening a test, for example by skipping it or deleting an assertion.
The share of a routine's last 20 closed PRs that people merged. Under half means people keep closing its work.

review.q: From memory: the three things a routine needs before its owner is told it qualifies for the next stage.
review.a: Its bench slice at least 50% solved (bug fixers also 60% reproduced), zero false heals, and at least 10 runs at its current stage.

review.q: The daily job finds a revert of a routine's PR from last week. Walk through what happens, in order, and who hears about it.
review.a: demotionReason returns the revert. The job writes the stage_override flag one step lower, so the next run uses it, opens a PR that lowers stage: in the charter, and sends the owner a message with the reason.

review.q: Why is shadow worth running at all, when it opens nothing?
review.a: It runs the real routine on real triggers and saves its fix, so the weekly report and the bench give evidence of how good it is, without costing anyone's attention or trust.

remember: A routine starts silent in shadow, moves up only on evidence and a person's reviewed yes, and steps down at once on the first bad sign.
